name: Spawn Object
desc: Spawns a non-living entity: item drop, boat, minecart, arrow, fireball, ender pearl, armor stand, etc.
notes: Entity types: 1=boat, 2=item, 50=TNTPrimed, 51=enderCrystal, 60=arrow, 61=snowball, 62=egg, 63=fireball, 64=smallFireball, 65=enderPearl, 66=witherSkull, 67=shulkerBullet, 68=llamaSpit, 90=fishingFloat, 91=spectralArrow, 93=dragonFireball. Used by AntiFireball (attack fireballs), ItemESP (track items), and BoatFly.

writeup.p: The spawn packet for every non-living entity: item drops (type 2), boats (1), minecarts (10), TNT (50), ender crystals (51), arrows and spectral arrows (60/91), snowballs (61), eggs (62), fireballs and small fireballs (63/64), ender pearls (65), wither skulls (66), fishing hooks (90), falling blocks (70), item frames (71), armor stands (78) and more. The server's EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket builds it with the EntityList type code, fixed-point position (x32), byte rotations (x256/360) and short velocity (x8000), and the third constructor argument packs a per-type data int: the shooter entity id for arrows and fireballs, the block state id for falling blocks, the minecart type for carts, the facing index for item frames.

NetHandlerPlayClient.handleSpawnObject reads the entity id, type byte, position, three rotations, the three velocity shorts and the trailing DataWatcher, then creates the entity through EntityList.createEntityByID and applies the transform. For projectile types the data int is used to look up the throwing entity so the client can attribute the projectile. Server side, the same packet class is the output of EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket, which is why the type codes and the data int semantics are defined by the server's tracking code, not by the packet class itself.

None of the 8 reference clients hook S0E in any module. The corpus shows only vanilla files plus Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 NetworkAPI.java, which lists S0EPacketSpawnObject in the packet registry that the scripting API exposes to scripts. The absence is structural: ESP, Tracers and KillAura in these clients iterate world.getLoadedEntityList on render ticks instead of hooking spawn packets, so they never see S0E, and the throwable-specific combat modules of the wider ecosystem (AntiFireball-style projectile attackers, item ESP) are not present in this corpus.

The packet is server-trusted end to end, so the attack surface is client-side robustness: extreme velocity shorts, bogus type codes and oversized DataWatcher payloads are the classic crash vectors, and armor stand floods (type 78) were the 1.8-era lag exploit. For anti-cheat work the interesting field is the data int: a projectile carrying the player's entity id as owner is the standard signal AntiFireball-style modules use, and servers that simulate projectiles server-side validate the owner id against the tracker. Anti-cheats that replay or predict projectile trajectories reconstruct them from S0E position and velocity, so the packet is a timing reference for those checks.

implementation.overview: The spawn packet for all non-living entities: items, vehicles, TNT, projectiles, armor stands. In the 8-client corpus it is untouched by modules: ESP iterates the world entity list instead of hooking spawn packets, and the only non-vanilla reference is Rise's NetworkAPI script registry. Documented for protocol completeness and for the projectile-attribution semantics modules in other ecosystems build on.
implementation.server_handling: EntityTrackerEntry.getPacket switches on the tracked entity class and returns S0E with a type code from EntityList, position x32, yaw/pitch byte rotations and motion x8000 shorts. The third constructor int is type-specific: shooter entity id for arrows and fireballs (0 when the shooter is gone), block state id for falling blocks, minecart type id for carts, facing horizontal index for item frames. The client handler creates the entity and applies the transform; for arrows the data int resolves the thrower so the client can render the correct owner.
implementation.protocol_notes: Entity id and type are VarInt/unsigned byte; position is three ints at x32, rotations are three bytes at x256/360 (yaw, pitch, head pitch), velocity is three shorts at x8000. A DataWatcher block terminates the packet only when the entity has metadata; most non-living types send an empty watcher. The same type codes are shared with the 1.8 EntityList server-side table, so a mismatch between client and server entity registries despawns the entity silently.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Nothing client-controlled is flaggable here because the packet is purely clientbound and server-authored. Anti-cheats use it indirectly: projectile simulation checks reconstruct arrow and fireball paths from S0E and replay them to catch players who dodge impossibly, and servers rate-limit object spawns to stop item/armor stand flood lag exploits. No reference client touches it, so there is no bypass trade-off to document beyond the generic entity-spawn flood mitigations.
implementation.client_variations: The only client-side difference in the corpus is Rise 6.1.30/6.2.4 exposing S0EPacketSpawnObject.class in NetworkAPI's packet list for the scripting system; every other client reference is the bundled vanilla NetHandlerPlayClient, EntityTrackerEntry, EnumConnectionState and INetHandlerPlayClient.
